properties.name: ROOT CAUSE — the server's 459 MB is glibc arena retention from the EXPORT path, not RocksDB. Opening the store costs 43 MB; five exports cost 293 MB, and MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 halves it
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-09-13 on this box, following the root-cause skill. Three arms, each a separate process on its own identical copy of reflow2's own 4,403-node store (14.7 MB export document), release binary, --serve-shared, glibc malloc.

① THE OBSERVATION, and the bound that did the most work:

    process that does NOT open a store   (--shared, --only-if-present)     19 MB
    server, store freshly opened, idle                                     62 MB
    live server, same design, hours of session use                        459 MB
    live server with --export-to, same design                             721 MB

Opening the store costs 43 MB over the store-less floor. The other ~400 MB accrues with USE.

② WHAT THIS REFUTES, including the hypothesis it was raised from:

 🛑 NOT THE ROCKSDB COLUMN-FAMILY DEFAULTS. flo2's handoff named this the headline — six ALL_CFS families at Options::default(), "~384 MB of memtable before anything else." A fresh server on the identical store with those exact defaults is 62 MB. The arithmetic is sound about the write-buffer BUDGET and wrong about resident cost, because RocksDB fills memtable arenas lazily. Tuning write_buffer_size, a shared block cache and max_open_files addresses the 43 MB, not the 400 MB.

 🛑 NOT THE FULL-TEXT INDEX. The tantivy writer arena is 50 MB by default and already runtime-tunable via DYNOGRAPH_FULLTEXT_WRITER_HEAP_MB. Flooring it at 15 MB moved nothing: 62 MB (default) against 68 MB (floored), the floored arm HIGHER. Candidate refuted by the measurement that could have confirmed it.

③ WHAT IT IS. Progressive load on one arm, measured after each stage:

    open store                                     62 MB
    + 10 x graph_report (18 KB replies)           101 MB
    + 30 x create_node                            140 MB
    + 5 x export_graph (14.7 MB replies)          433 MB   <- +293 MB
    + 10 more exports                         504-542 MB   (oscillating, not climbing)

④ LEAK OR RETENTION — separated, and it is retention. Exports 6-15 move 535, 539, 542, 504, 504, 504, 504, 542, 542, 542. A leak does not go down. The working set per export is large (the whole document materialized in memory, plus serialization buffers), freed to the allocator, and not returned to the OS.

⑤ THE DISCRIMINATING ARM. Same everything, MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2: 60 MB baseline, 233 MB after five exports, against 433 MB unset. glibc's per-thread arena count is the retaining mechanism, and one environment variable takes ~200 MB off at this workload.

⑥ THE CLASS, not the instance. export_graph is the largest instance, not the whole of it — the ten reads that added 39 MB are the same shape at smaller scale. The class is: a long-lived server that materializes large per-call payloads, under a multi-arena allocator that retains freed blocks. Bounding only export_graph would leave the class open, which is the failure fact:the-parallel-batch-class-recurred-because-only-its-instance-was-fixed already records here.

⑨ WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED — and the first item matters most:

 ⚠️ THIS DOES NOT EXPLAIN FLO2'S NUMBER. Their 448 MB was on a 202-node / 2.9 MB design, whose export is a fraction of this one's. The same mechanism at that size should cost far less. Either their server did something the handoff does not describe, or their number has a different cause. It is unexplained and must not be treated as covered by this.
 · Throughput under MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 was NOT measured. Fewer arenas means more contention between threads; this trades one for the other and only one side has been measured.
 · jemalloc and mimalloc were not tried, and neither was an explicit malloc_trim after export. Whether a different allocator beats the env var is unknown.
 · Whether the export path could stream the document instead of materializing it whole was not examined. That would attack the peak rather than the retention.
 · Measured on glibc/Linux only. The published image's base libc was not checked, and musl's allocator behaves differently.
 · No test pins this yet. Step 7 of the discipline is not done.
